title: Back on track
claim: A 12-week supervised exercise programme improves physical function in adults with chronic low back pain.

question.submitted: Does a 12-week exercise programme improve function in chronic low back pain, compared with usual care?

facts.sound: Registered before the first patient, with function at 12 weeks as primary outcome, as in the paper.

flaw.text: Registered with pain at 12 weeks as primary outcome. The paper makes function primary and never says why.
flaw.why: Switching the primary outcome after seeing the data lets a chance finding pass as the main result. Fixable: report the registered outcome as primary and explain the change.

facts.sound: Hypothesis stated: the programme improves the function score by at least 3 points more than usual care.

method.submitted: Randomised trial in four clinics; patients allocated 1:1 to supervised exercise or usual care.

facts.sound: Computer-made sequence in random blocks, released by a central web service only after enrolment.

flaw.text: Patients seen on Mondays and Wednesdays got exercise; patients seen on other days got usual care.
flaw.why: Staff could foresee each allocation and steer who was enrolled on which day, so the groups may differ from the start. No reanalysis can undo that.

facts.sound: Two supervised sessions a week for 12 weeks; the full exercise protocol is in a supplement.

flaw.text: Described only as 'supervised exercise, twice a week'; the exercises, intensity and progression are not given.
flaw.why: This gap doesn't bias the comparison, but nobody can repeat the programme or offer it to patients. Minor: describe it in full (TIDieR), for example in a supplement.

sample.submitted: 240 adults with low back pain for more than 3 months, referred by their GPs.

facts.sound: All consecutive referrals screened against published criteria; 240 of 412 eligible and consenting.

flaw.text: Physiotherapists enrolled only patients they judged 'motivated to exercise'; no written criteria.
flaw.why: Randomisation still balances the groups, so the comparison is fair, but the result may not apply to typical patients. Minor: report it and narrow the claims.

facts.sound: Flow diagram: 412 screened, 240 randomised, 226 with a 12-week score; losses similar per arm, with reasons.

flaw.text: No flow diagram: 240 were randomised, but losses are not given per arm or with reasons.
flaw.why: Few were lost (14 of 240, 6%) and the missing-data analysis covers them, but readers need to see who left each arm and why. Minor: add the CONSORT flow diagram.

measurement.submitted: Function scored with a standard performance test at 12 weeks.

facts.sound: Tests scored by assessors from another clinic who did not know anyone's group.

flaw.text: Each patient's own physiotherapist scored the test, knowing who had the exercise programme.
flaw.why: Assessors who know the groups tend to see the effect they expect. A 12-week performance test can't be repeated blind afterwards, so the main result can't be rescued.

facts.sound: The performance test has published reliability and validity in low back pain.

analysis.submitted: Groups compared with a linear model adjusted for baseline function.

facts.sound: 6% of outcomes missing, handled by multiple imputation; complete-case results agree.
Every randomised patient analysed in the group they were assigned to.

flaw.text: Only patients who attended at least 80% of sessions were analysed: 61 of 120 in the exercise arm.
flaw.why: Dropping non-adherers breaks randomisation: people who keep exercising differ from those who stop. Fixable: reanalyse everyone as randomised (intention to treat).

title: Late-night scrolling
claim: Heavy social-media use at age 13 predicts sleep problems at age 15.

question.submitted: Does heavy social-media use at age 13 predict sleep problems at age 15?

facts.sound: Hypothesis from the funded proposal, cited: more daily use, more sleep problems at 15, in girls and boys alike.

flaw.text: The introduction predicts an effect in girls only. The proposal predicted it for everyone; only girls showed it.
flaw.why: A hypothesis written after the results makes a chance subgroup finding look like a confirmed prediction. Fixable: restore the original hypothesis and label the girls-only result exploratory.

facts.sound: Not preregistered; the authors say so plainly in the limitations.

method.submitted: Prospective school-based cohort with questionnaires at ages 13 and 15.

facts.sound: Use measured at 13 and sleep at 15, two years apart, at the same point in the school year.

flaw.text: Both were asked at 15: pupils recalled how much they had used social media two years earlier.
flaw.why: Use at 13 is recalled after the sleep problems began, so the timing that made it a prediction is gone. Only data collected at 13 could fix this.

sample.submitted: 3,000 pupils from 40 schools enrolled at 13; 2,310 followed up at 15.

facts.sound: Losses shown by school and reason; leavers and stayers had similar use and sleep at 13.

flaw.text: Heavy users were twice as likely to be lost by 15; leavers and stayers are never compared.
flaw.why: If the heavy users who left slept differently, the estimate is biased. Fixable: compare leavers with stayers and correct with weighting or imputation.

facts.sound: Size set by the parent cohort; the paper reports the precision this gives the main estimate.

flaw.text: The paper doesn't say how the cohort size was set, or what precision it gives the main estimate.
flaw.why: The parent cohort fixed the size, so the data stand; readers need only that sentence and the estimate's confidence interval. Minor: explain how the size was set.

measurement.submitted: Sleep problems at 15 measured by questionnaire.

facts.sound: A validated adolescent sleep questionnaire, plus a week of wrist actigraphy in a subsample.

flaw.text: One yes/no item written for this study, 'Do you often sleep badly?', with no validation.
flaw.why: One home-made yes/no item can't show it measures sleep problems. Fixable in part: use the cohort's fuller sleep measures, or validate the item in a subsample, and temper the claims.

analysis.submitted: Logistic regression of sleep problems on hours of use, adjusted for confounders.

facts.sound: Results hold with use in hours per day and with cut-offs at 2, 3 and 4 hours.

flaw.text: Use was split at 3 hours after trying cut-offs from 1 to 5; only the one with p < 0.05 is reported.
flaw.why: Trying many cut-offs and reporting the one that works inflates false positives. Fixable: analyse hours as a continuous measure, or show every cut-off.

facts.sound: Adjusted for sleep, mood and family income at 13, chosen in advance from a causal diagram.

flaw.text: Adjusted for sleep, mood and income at 13, but only the adjusted odds ratio and a p-value are given.
flaw.why: A p-value says nothing about how large or how precise the effect is, and without the unadjusted estimate readers can't see what adjustment changed. Minor: report both, with 95% confidence intervals.

title: Sleeping pills and hip fracture
claim: Benzodiazepine use doubles the risk of hip fracture in people over 70.

question.submitted: Does benzodiazepine use raise the risk of hip fracture in people over 70?

facts.sound: Protocol hypothesis: benzodiazepine use raises hip-fracture risk. The paper tests that one question.

flaw.text: Nine sleep medicines were tested. The headline is the one significant drug, with no correction for nine tests.
flaw.why: With nine tests, one 'significant' result is likely by chance alone. Fixable: report all nine, correct for multiple testing, and call the single-drug finding exploratory.

method.submitted: Case-control study: 400 hip-fracture cases and 800 matched controls from two regions.

facts.sound: Drug use counted only in the year before each case's fracture date, with the same window for its controls.

flaw.text: Drug use counted from 6 months before to 1 month after the fracture, when many start sleeping pills in hospital.
flaw.why: Pills started because of the fracture are counted as its cause. Fixable: rerun the analysis with use before the fracture date only.

sample.submitted: Cases from hospital admissions; controls matched on age and sex.

facts.sound: Controls drawn at random from the same regions' population register.

flaw.text: Controls were volunteers recruited at senior fitness clubs.
flaw.why: Fitness-club members take fewer sleeping pills and fall less than the population the cases came from, so the comparison is biased from the start. New controls are needed.

facts.sound: 81% of cases and 76% of controls took part; reasons for refusal are reported.

ref.cite: Vandenbroucke et al. (2007). Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE): explanation and elaboration. PLoS Medicine.

flaw.text: Participation given only overall ('about 80%'), not for cases and controls separately; no reasons for refusal.
flaw.why: Bias arises if taking part depends on pill use differently in cases and controls; per-group rates and reasons are the first check. Minor: report them per group; here they are similar (81% and 76%).

measurement.submitted: Benzodiazepine use assessed in the same way for cases and controls.

facts.sound: Use taken from pharmacy dispensing records for cases and controls alike.

flaw.text: Use recalled in interviews: cases on the ward days after their fracture, controls by phone.
flaw.why: Cases search their memory harder, in a different setting, so their use is over-reported. Fixable in part: check the answers against pharmacy records.

facts.sound: Records abstracted by staff who did not know who was a case.

analysis.submitted: Conditional logistic regression, adjusted for other risk factors.

facts.sound: Adjusted for dementia, frailty, previous falls and other fall-risk drugs, chosen in advance.

flaw.text: Adjusted for age and sex only. Dementia and frailty, which lead to both pills and falls, are ignored.
flaw.why: Frail people get more sleeping pills and fall more, so part of the 'drug effect' may be frailty. Fixable if the data hold these factors: adjust for them and show both estimates.

facts.sound: Results similar when restricted to new users and to fractures from simple falls.

flaw.text: 'Sensitivity analyses confirmed the results', the paper says, without saying which analyses or showing them.
flaw.why: Readers can't tell what was checked, or how closely it agreed. Minor: describe each sensitivity analysis and show its results, for example in a supplement.

title: Burnout in the doctorate
claim: Almost half of PhD students are burnt out, and poor supervision causes it.

question.submitted: How common is burnout among PhD students, and what is it associated with?

facts.sound: Aims: estimate prevalence and describe associations. The conclusion stays descriptive.

flaw.text: The aim is descriptive, yet the abstract concludes that poor supervision causes burnout.
flaw.why: A one-off survey can't show which came first, burnout or poor supervision. Minor: rewrite the conclusion as an association.

method.submitted: Online survey of PhD students at four universities in spring 2025.

facts.sound: Survey open for three weeks in March 2025, away from the main submission deadlines.

flaw.text: Dates given only as 'spring 2025'; when the survey opened and closed, and what fell in that window, isn't said.
flaw.why: Answers can shift with the academic calendar (exams, teaching, funding rounds), so readers need the exact window. Minor: give the opening and closing dates and what fell within them.

facts.sound: All 2,100 enrolled PhD students were invited by email, with two reminders.

flaw.text: The link was shared on a PhD well-being forum and on social media; anyone could answer.
flaw.why: Whether people answer depends on how much burnout matters to them, so the prevalence can't be generalised. A new, defined sample is needed.

facts.sound: Numbers who opened, started and finished the survey are reported, with the drop-off at each step.

measurement.submitted: Burnout measured with a questionnaire scored against a cut-off.

facts.sound: A validated burnout inventory, scored with the manual's published cut-off.

flaw.text: Five items written by the authors; 'burnout' means scoring above the midpoint; no validation.
flaw.why: A prevalence is only as good as the measure and its cut-off. Fixable only in part: give validity evidence, or report scores instead of a prevalence.

analysis.submitted: Prevalence with 95% confidence intervals; regression for associations.

facts.sound: 3% of items missing, prorated as the scale's manual specifies.

flaw.text: The 22% who skipped any item were dropped; skipping was commonest among those reporting long hours.
flaw.why: If the students under most pressure skipped items, dropping them biases the prevalence. Fixable: multiple imputation, and compare completers with non-completers.

facts.sound: Estimates weighted by faculty and sex give the same prevalence within 2 points.

flaw.text: Weighting by faculty and sex 'made no difference', the paper says, but the weighted estimates are not shown.
flaw.why: Readers can't see how big the difference was. Minor: show the weighted prevalence beside the unweighted one.

title: Moral distress in intensive care
claim: ICU nurses' moral distress centres on staffing, families and end-of-life decisions.

question.submitted: How do intensive-care nurses experience moral distress around end-of-life decisions?

facts.sound: An exploratory aim, stated up front, and no hypothesis, as suits an interview study.

method.submitted: Semi-structured interviews with ICU nurses at one university hospital.

facts.sound: Interviews by a researcher from another hospital with no role over the nurses; her nursing background is described.

flaw.text: Every interview was done by the unit's head nurse, who also writes the nurses' appraisals.
flaw.why: Nurses are unlikely to speak freely to the person who appraises them, so the data themselves are compromised. New interviews are needed.

sample.submitted: Fourteen nurses, chosen for a range of experience and shift patterns.

facts.sound: Interviews continued until three in a row added no new codes; the paper shows how this was judged.

flaw.text: Data collection stopped at 14 because the project ended. Saturation is claimed but not shown.
flaw.why: Saturation means new data stop adding insight, not that time ran out. Fixable: show how completeness was judged, or add interviews.

facts.sound: Purposive sampling by years of experience and shift pattern; 3 of 17 nurses approached declined.

flaw.text: Purposive sampling is named, but not how the nurses were approached, or by whom.
flaw.why: Readers can't judge whether the nurses felt free to say no. Minor: say who invited the nurses, and how.

measurement.submitted: Interviews audio-recorded, transcribed in full and coded.

facts.sound: Two researchers coded independently and met to settle differences; the coding tree is in a supplement.

flaw.text: One researcher coded every transcript. There is no coding tree and no second reader.
flaw.why: With one coder and no audit trail, readers can't judge how the codes came from the data. Fixable: a second coder, the coding tree and an audit trail.

facts.sound: The interview guide was piloted with two nurses and is given in full.

flaw.text: The guide's topics are listed, but its questions and prompts aren't given, and piloting isn't mentioned.
flaw.why: Readers can't see what the nurses were asked or how the questions framed their answers. Minor: give the guide in full and say whether it was piloted.

analysis.submitted: Reflexive thematic analysis produced four themes.

facts.sound: Themes were built from codes across interviews and checked against the full data set.

flaw.text: The four themes are the four headings of the interview guide, although the paper says they came from the data.
flaw.why: Using the interview questions as themes summarises the guide, not the data; Braun & Clarke (2006) name it a pitfall. Fixable: redo the analysis.

title: A scan for appendicitis
claim: Bedside ultrasound by emergency doctors detects appendicitis in children with 97% sensitivity.

question.submitted: How accurate is bedside ultrasound by emergency doctors for appendicitis in children?

facts.sound: Registered before recruitment, with the same target condition, population and cut-off as the paper.

flaw.text: Registered for patients of all ages. The paper reports children only and never mentions the adults.
flaw.why: Leaving out a registered group can hide results that didn't suit. Fixable: report the whole registered population, or explain why not.

facts.sound: Prespecified target: a sensitivity of at least 90%.

flaw.text: The aim is 'to assess accuracy'; no minimum acceptable sensitivity was set in advance.
flaw.why: Without a target, whether 97% is good enough is judged after the fact, but the estimate and its interval still stand. Minor: state that no target was set, and judge the lower confidence limit against what clinicians need.

method.submitted: Every child had a scan; the diagnosis was confirmed with a reference standard.

facts.sound: Histology if operated on; otherwise a phone follow-up at 14 days. The same rule for every child.

flaw.text: Only children with a positive scan had surgery and histology. Negatives went home without follow-up.
flaw.why: Missed cases among the negatives are never found, so sensitivity looks too high. Fixable only if follow-up can still be obtained for the negatives.

sample.submitted: Children aged 4 to 16 with abdominal pain, at two emergency departments.

facts.sound: Consecutive children with suspected appendicitis, on every shift.

flaw.text: Children with surgically confirmed appendicitis, compared with healthy children from a school check-up.
flaw.why: Comparing clear cases with healthy children leaves out the hard, look-alike cases, so accuracy is inflated. A new, clinically realistic sample is needed.

facts.sound: Flow diagram: 412 eligible, 398 scanned, 6 without a reference standard, each explained.

ref.cite: Cohen et al. (2016). STARD 2015 guidelines for reporting diagnostic accuracy studies: explanation and elaboration. BMJ Open.

flaw.text: No flow diagram: 398 children were scanned, but not how many were eligible, or why some lack a reference standard.
flaw.why: Readers can't tell who was never scanned or never verified, or whether they differ. Minor: add a STARD flow diagram with the reason for each child lost.

measurement.submitted: Each scan read as positive or negative for appendicitis.

facts.sound: Readers knew only the child's age and symptoms, not the lab results or the final diagnosis.

flaw.text: Stored scans were read after surgery, by doctors who knew the histology result.
flaw.why: Readers who know the answer read the scan in its light, which inflates accuracy. Fixable: re-read the stored scans blind.

analysis.submitted: Sensitivity and specificity with 95% confidence intervals.

facts.sound: Positive meant an appendix wider than 6 mm, a cut-off fixed in the protocol.

flaw.text: The 6 mm cut-off was picked after the data, as the one giving the best accuracy.
flaw.why: A cut-off tuned on the same data flatters accuracy. Fixable: use a prespecified cut-off, or validate this one in new data.

facts.sound: Inconclusive scans (9%) counted as negative, and as positive in a sensitivity analysis.

title: Mindfulness apps for anxiety
claim: Mindfulness apps reduce anxiety in adults, with a moderate pooled effect.

question.submitted: Do mindfulness apps reduce anxiety in adults, compared with control conditions?

facts.sound: Registered on PROSPERO before screening; outcomes and methods match the paper.

flaw.text: PROSPERO lists depression as the primary outcome. The review leads with anxiety and doesn't say why.
flaw.why: Choosing the headline outcome after seeing the results lets the best-looking one win. Fixable: report the registered outcome first and explain the change.

facts.sound: Question in PICO form: adults, app-based mindfulness, any control, anxiety symptoms.

method.submitted: Systematic search for randomised trials, screened by two reviewers.

facts.sound: Five databases and two trial registers, no language limits; full search strings in a supplement.

flaw.text: PubMed only, English only, no trial registers; the search string isn't given.
flaw.why: One database misses many trials, and the missed ones are not a random set. Fixable: redo the search across several sources.

sample.submitted: 23 randomised trials with 4,380 adults were included.

facts.sound: Any randomised trial was eligible, published or not, including register results and theses.

flaw.text: Only trials published in journals were eligible; register results and theses were excluded.
flaw.why: Unpublished trials more often find no effect, so leaving them out inflates the pooled effect. Fixable: widen eligibility and look for them.

facts.sound: PRISMA flow diagram: 1,204 records, 61 full texts, 23 included; every exclusion has a reason.

ref.cite: Page et al. (2021). PRISMA 2020 explanation and elaboration: updated guidance and exemplars for reporting systematic reviews. BMJ.

flaw.text: Only the 23 included trials are listed: no flow diagram, no count of records screened, no reasons for exclusion.
flaw.why: Readers can't check the selection or spot trials wrongly left out. Minor: add a PRISMA flow diagram with a reason for each full text excluded.

measurement.submitted: Results and study quality extracted by two reviewers.

facts.sound: Two reviewers applied RoB 2 to each trial independently; judgements shown domain by domain.

flaw.text: No risk-of-bias tool was used; trials were called 'high quality' because they were peer-reviewed.
flaw.why: Without judging each trial's bias, nobody can tell whether the effect rests on weak trials. Fixable: assess with RoB 2 and run a sensitivity analysis by risk of bias.

analysis.submitted: Random-effects meta-analysis of standardised mean differences.

facts.sound: I² = 34%; a subgroup analysis by type of control was planned and reported.

flaw.text: I² = 89%, yet one pooled effect is presented as the answer, and the differences are not explored.
flaw.why: When trials disagree this much, one average may describe none of them. Fixable: explore the causes (subgroups, meta-regression) and temper the summary.

facts.sound: Funnel plot and Egger's test across the 23 trials show no clear asymmetry.

flaw.text: Funnel plot and Egger's test show no clear asymmetry, so the review concludes there is 'no publication bias'.
flaw.why: These tests can miss bias, and a symmetrical funnel can't prove that no studies are missing. Minor: reword as 'no clear evidence of small-study effects'.

title: A drug for stroke mice
claim: Compound NR-4, given after a stroke, cuts brain damage in mice by 40%.

question.submitted: Does compound NR-4, given after a stroke, reduce brain damage in mice?

facts.sound: Protocol registered beforehand, with infarct volume at 72 hours as primary outcome, as reported.

flaw.text: Registered with a 24-hour behaviour score as primary. The paper reports infarct volume and omits the behaviour score.
flaw.why: Dropping the registered outcome hides a result that may not have suited. Fixable: report the behaviour score and explain the switch.

facts.sound: Hypothesis stated: NR-4 reduces infarct volume at 72 hours compared with vehicle.

method.submitted: Mice with an induced stroke received NR-4 or vehicle one hour later.

facts.sound: Computer-made random list, held by a colleague who did no surgery.

flaw.text: The first mice taken out of each cage got NR-4; the rest got vehicle.
flaw.why: The mice caught first can differ (calmer, slower, smaller), so the groups may differ before treatment. The experiment has to be repeated with random allocation.

facts.sound: Dose, route, timing, vehicle and anaesthesia described; the vehicle looked identical.

flaw.text: Dose and timing are given; the route, the vehicle and the anaesthesia are not described.
flaw.why: Readers can't check that both groups were handled alike, and nobody can repeat the experiment exactly. Minor: report route, vehicle and anaesthesia, as ARRIVE item 9 asks.

sample.submitted: Twelve mice per group, as planned.

facts.sound: All 24 mice analysed; no deaths and no exclusions.

flaw.text: Five NR-4 mice died or were excluded; they were replaced and are not mentioned.
flaw.why: Replacing animals that died hides harm and can leave only the mice that responded. Fixable: report every animal and analyse with the losses included.

facts.sound: Power calculation from pilot data: 12 per group to detect a 30% reduction.

flaw.text: Twelve per group, 'as is usual in the field'; no sample size calculation is reported.
flaw.why: Small studies that reach significance tend to overstate the effect, and readers can't tell what this one was designed to detect. Minor: say how 12 was chosen, and give the 40% with its 95% confidence interval.

measurement.submitted: Infarct volume measured on stained brain slices at 72 hours.

facts.sound: Slices were coded; the person measuring them did not know the groups.

flaw.text: The researcher who dosed the mice also measured the slices, knowing each group.
flaw.why: Tracing infarct edges takes judgement that expectations can sway. Fixable here, unlike in a live test: the stored slices can be re-measured blind.

facts.sound: Infarct volume defined in the methods and corrected for brain swelling.

analysis.submitted: Groups compared with a t-test; p < 0.001.

facts.sound: Each mouse counted once, with its slices averaged: 12 per group.

flaw.text: Each brain slice counted as a separate observation: 120 slices instead of 24 mice.
flaw.why: Slices from one mouse are not independent, so the p-value is far too small. Fixable: reanalyse with the mouse as the unit.
